sections.text: ## The Big Picture

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
Convolution and correlation are the fundamental operations of LTI signal processing.
Convolution IS filtering. Correlation IS similarity measurement.

```
sections.text: ## Linear Convolution

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
For sequences x[n] of length M and h[n] of length L:
- Output y[n] = x[n] ★ h[n] has length M + L - 1
- Linear convolution is acyclic (no wraparound)

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
```
LINEAR CONVOLUTION EXAMPLE
x = [1, 2, 3]   (M=3)
h = [1, 1]      (L=2)

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text: Method: flip h, slide over x, multiply and sum at each position:

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide
Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide
Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
**Graphical interpretation**: Convolution is the area of overlap between x and a
flipped, sliding version of h as a function of offset n.

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
**Properties**:
- Commutativity: x ★ h = h ★ x
- Associativity: (x ★ h₁) ★ h₂ = x ★ (h₁ ★ h₂)  (cascade = single filter)
- Distributivity: x ★ (h₁ + h₂) = (x ★ h₁) + (x ★ h₂)  (parallel = add filters)
- Identity: x ★ δ = x  (delta is identity for convolution)

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide
Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text: ## Circular Convolution

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text: DFT-based convolution is inherently circular — it assumes the signal is periodic with period N.

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
```
LINEAR vs CIRCULAR (N-point DFT)

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
Linear convolution:     y_lin[n] = Σ x[k]·h[n-k],  length = M+L-1
                                    k

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
Circular convolution:   y_circ[n] = Σ x[k]·h[(n-k) mod N]
                                      k

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
PROBLEM: If N < M+L-1, the circular convolution wraps around:
  y_lin   = [1, 3, 5, 3,  0,  0, ...]  (linear, zero tail)
  y_circ  = [1+3, 3+0, 5+0, 3+0] = [4, 3, 5, 3]  for N=4
             └── aliasing from wrap! ─┘

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
SOLUTION: Zero-pad both x and h to length ≥ M+L-1 before DFT.
Then circular convolution equals linear convolution.
```

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
**DFT-based filtering**:
```
y = IFFT{ FFT{x} × FFT{h} }   with N ≥ M+L-1
```
Complexity: O(N log N) vs O(N²) for direct method.

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide
Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text: ## Long-Input Convolution: Overlap-Add / Overlap-Save

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
For streaming audio/real-time filtering, input x is continuous (infinite) while filter h has
finite length L. Process in blocks.

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
```
OVERLAP-ADD METHOD

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
Filter h: length L
Input x: broken into blocks of length M (non-overlapping)

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
For each block xₖ:
1. Zero-pad xₖ to length N ≥ M+L-1
2. FFT(xₖ) × FFT(h)  (precompute FFT of h)
3. IFFT → yₖ of length N = M+L-1
4. Each yₖ output has L-1 samples of "tail" that overlap with next block
5. Add overlapping parts → correct linear convolution output

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
OUTPUT ASSEMBLY:
Block 1:  [────────────────────]tail₁
Block 2:  [────────────────────]tail₂
                            tail₁+[tail of block2 start]
```

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
```
OVERLAP-SAVE METHOD (more common in practice)

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
Keep a sliding buffer of length N = M+L-1 (overlapping input)
1. Fill buffer (L-1 old samples + M new samples)
2. Compute N-point FFT of buffer
3. Multiply by H[k]
4. IFFT
5. Discard first L-1 samples (they contain circular aliasing)
6. Output M valid samples
7. Slide buffer: keep last L-1 samples for next block
```

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
**Computational cost**: N = M+L-1 ≈ next power of 2.
For M=1024 input block, L=256 filter: N=2048, cost ≈ 2048·log₂(2048)/1024 ≈ 22 mults/sample.
Compare: direct convolution = 256 mults/sample. 11× speedup.

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide
Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text: ## Cross-Correlation

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text: Cross-correlation measures the similarity between x and y as a function of time lag τ:

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
```
Rxy[n] = Σ x[k] · y[k+n] = Σ x[k] · y[k+n]
          k                  k

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text: or equivalently: Rxy[n] = x[-n] ★ y[n]  (convolution with x reversed)

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
Normalized: ρxy[n] = Rxy[n] / √(Rxx[0]·Ryy[0])   ∈ [-1, +1]
```

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
**Key insight**: Rxy[n] peaks at n = n₀ when y is a delayed copy of x by n₀ samples.
This gives the time delay estimate.

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
**Applications**:
- **Radar/sonar**: transmitted pulse correlated with received echo → range
- **Time delay estimation**: two microphones, find which signal arrived first
- **GPS**: known C/A code correlated with received signal → time of arrival → position
- **Vibration analysis**: find resonances, transfer functions

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide
Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text: ## Autocorrelation

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text: Autocorrelation is cross-correlation of a signal with itself:

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
```
Rxx[n] = Σ x[k] · x[k+n]
          k

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
PROPERTIES:
• Rxx[0] = Σ|x[k]|² = signal energy (peak at zero lag)
• Rxx[n] = Rxx[-n]  (even function, symmetric)
• |Rxx[n]| ≤ Rxx[0] for all n
• For periodic x with period P: Rxx[n] is also periodic with period P

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
FOURIER PAIR:
F{Rxx[n]} = |X(f)|² = Power Spectral Density (PSD)
→ Wiener-Khinchin theorem (see 06-STOCHASTIC)
```

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide
Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text: ## Matched Filter

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text: The matched filter maximizes SNR at a specific time instant in the presence of white noise.

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
```
MATCHED FILTER DESIGN

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
Given known signal s[n] of length L contaminated by noise:
Received: x[n] = α·s[n - n₀] + w[n]   (delayed signal + white noise)

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
Optimal filter: h[n] = s[L-1-n]  (time-reversed version of s)
Filter output: y[n] = x[n] ★ h[n] = Rsx[n]  (cross-correlation)

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
At n = n₀ + L - 1:
  Signal term: α · Rss[0] = α · ∫|s|²   (maximum possible, by Cauchy-Schwarz)
  Noise term:  minimum

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text: Peak SNR = 2·E_s / N₀   where E_s = signal energy, N₀ = noise PSD

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
RADAR PULSE COMPRESSION:
Transmit long coded pulse (high energy) → correlate with replica →
detect narrow pulse (high range resolution) with full energy
This is why radar waveforms are designed for good autocorrelation properties
(low sidelobes) — LFM chirp, phase-coded sequences (Barker codes, Gold codes).
```

sections.text: ## Bridge: CNN Layers as Learned FIR Filter Banks

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text: A CNN convolutional layer IS a bank of FIR filters with learned coefficients:

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
```
DSP CONVOLUTION              CNN "CONVOLUTION"
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FIR filter h[n]              Kernel weights w[k] (3×3, 5×5, etc.)
Convolution y = h * x        Forward pass y = w ⊛ x (actually cross-correlation —
  (flip h, slide, dot)          ML libraries don't flip the kernel)
Filter bank (parallel FIRs)  Multiple output channels = multiple learned filters
Downsampling by M            Stride = M (skip M positions between outputs)
Filter design (Parks-McCl)   Backpropagation (gradient descent on w)
```

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text: The forward pass in a CNN is cross-correlation, not convolution — `torch.nn.Conv2d` does NOT flip the kernel. For symmetric kernels this doesn't matter; for asymmetric ones the distinction is real. In classical DSP the flip is essential for the associativity property (cascade of filters); in ML the kernel is learned end-to-end so the flip is irrelevant.

sections.text: ## Decision Cheat Sheet

metadata.title: Convolution and Correlation - A Layered Guide

sections.text:
| If you need to diagnose... | Start With | Key Caveat |
|---|---|---|
| Short FIR filtering | Direct convolution by sum products | Simpler and often faster than FFT once setup overhead dominates. |
| Long streaming FIR filtering | Overlap-save or overlap-add | Block boundaries require correct padding and discard/keep rules. |
| Long filter by long signal | FFT-domain multiply followed by IFFT | Zero-pad to at least `M + L - 1` or circular wrap aliases the result. |
| Known signal in noise | Matched filter by correlating with the replica | Maximizes output SNR, not range/time resolution. |
| Time-delay estimation | Cross-correlation peak | High correlation indicates predictability at lag, not causality. |
| Signal energy measurement | Autocorrelation at lag 0 | Scaling convention determines whether the value is energy, power, or biased estimate. |
| Periodicity detection | Autocorrelation recurring peaks | Periodic peaks can also arise from repeated artifacts or windowing. |
| 2D image filtering | 2D convolution, separable when kernel permits | Convolution flips the kernel; correlation-like implementations may differ at asymmetric edges. |
